In progressMSc dissertation · GT-Power + MATLAB/Simulink co-simulation

Electrified torque assistance for knock-limited SI engine transients

In a high-performance spark-ignition engine, knock forces the spark to retard during a transient and the driver feels a torque deficit while the spark recovers. An electric motor can fill that gap. The study asks how the assist should be controlled and sized to cut the deficit and speed the recovery, within knock, e-machine and electrical-energy limits.

Research questions

  • RQ1 How large is the knock-induced torque deficit, and how does it scale with transient severity?
  • RQ2 How do fixed and adaptive (knock-triggered) assist strategies compare across three control cases?
  • RQ3 What is the minimum-energy assist for two to three representative transients? Bounded on purpose, not a full optimisation campaign.

Where it stands

  • Built: baseline GT-Power engine model (1-D engine plant).
  • Built: adaptive, knock-triggered e-motor assist model coupled to the engine in co-simulation.
  • Next: control-case runs, sensitivity analysis, bounded optimisation, and experimental correlation if test data access is confirmed.
  • Motor and battery reference values come from FIA F1 and Le Mans Hypercar technical regulations, used as realistic generic limits rather than a model of one car.
ΔT(t) = Tref(t) − Tice,knock(t)Torque deficit
0 ≤ Tm ≤ Tm,max(ω)   Pm = Tmω ≤ Pm,maxMotor limits
Pbatt = Pmηsys   SOCmin ≤ SOC ≤ SOCmaxBattery side
min J = ∫0tf Pbatt dt   s.t. ΔTres ≤ εMinimum-energy objective

These equations are the formulation the study is set up around. Results are not reported until the runs are complete.

In progressMSc project · Simcenter STAR-CCM+ · in-cylinder RANS CFD · ECN / Sandia data

Hydrogen direct injection: how tumble shapes the mixture

Direct injection after intake valve closure stops backfire and raises power density, but leaves little time for hydrogen to mix. I am building a 3D moving-mesh CFD model of the ECN hydrogen optical engine at Sandia, validating it against published PIV and PLIF measurements at two tumble ratios (0.22 and 0.70), and then using it to quantify how intake tumble changes the mixture before ignition.

0.25 → 0.94Mixture uniformity index on the PLIF plane, −130 to −30 °CA (measured data, high tumble)
−85 °CA99% of the plane already flammable (φ ≥ 0.1)
Sign reversalIn-plane tumble estimate reverses by −55 °CA: the jet overrides the intake vortex
~8 cm³Clearance-volume error found in the public CAD, corrected before meshing

Part A, analysis of the Sandia data in Python, is complete. CFD validation and the tumble sweep are in progress.

CompleteGT-POWER · 1-D · 2.0 L SI · 6000 rpm · 3 cases

Gasoline vs E20 in a 2.0 L spark-ignition engine

What does an E20 blend cost an engine calibrated for gasoline, and what does the ECU need to change to recover it? I modelled the engine on gasoline (indolene) and on E20 at 6000 rpm in three cases: fixed air-fuel ratio, corrected stoichiometric AFR (13.60), and the calibration implications for non-flex-fuel and flex-fuel vehicles.

−2.2%Brake power, E20 with AFR corrected to 13.60, against gasoline
29.7 to 29.5%Brake thermal efficiency, gasoline to E20. Essentially flat.
+9.1%Brake specific fuel consumption penalty
CO, HC lowerQualitative. NOx depends on engine calibration.
Model results at 6000 rpm
ParameterGasolineE20
Brake power96.2 kW94.1 kW
Brake torque153.2 N·m149.8 N·m
Air-fuel ratio14.5113.60
Fuel flow26.7 kg/h28.5 kg/h
BSFC277.7 g/kW·h303.0 g/kW·h
Brake efficiency29.7%29.5%
BSECabout 12.1 MJ/kWhabout 12.2 MJ/kWh

The fuel: E20

E20 is gasoline blended with 20% ethanol by volume, which is about 21% by mass. Ethanol is an oxygenated fuel: it carries oxygen in the molecule, holds less energy per kilogram and needs less air to burn. It also has a much higher latent heat of vaporisation and a higher octane rating, so it cools the charge and resists knock better than gasoline.

Typical handbook values, blend by mass
PropertyGasolineEthanolE20
Lower heating value, MJ/kgabout 43about 27about 40
Stoichiometric AFRabout 14.69.0about 13.4
Oxygen by mass0%about 35%about 7%
Latent heat, kJ/kgabout 350about 900about 460

The model used AFR 14.51 for gasoline and 13.60 for E20. E20 values are mass-weighted blends of the first two columns.

Brake specific energy consumption

BSEC is the fuel energy burned per unit of brake work. It is BSFC multiplied by the fuel's heating value, so it compares fuels fairly even when their energy content differs. It is also the inverse of brake thermal efficiency, so a flat BSEC means flat efficiency.

In the model BSEC was about 12.1 MJ/kWh on gasoline and about 12.2 MJ/kWh on E20. The 9.1% BSFC rise is almost entirely the lower energy content of E20, not a worse engine. A check against the table: 3.6 / 12.1 = 29.75% and 3.6 / 12.2 = 29.5%, matching the 29.7% and 29.5% efficiencies within rounding.

Reading the result

Ethanol holds less energy per kilogram than gasoline, about 27 against 43 MJ/kg using typical handbook values. E20 is roughly 21% ethanol by mass, so its heating value is about 7 to 8% lower. Brake thermal efficiency is power divided by fuel energy flow. With efficiency flat and energy per kilogram down, fuel mass flow has to rise, and that is the BSFC penalty. The 8 to 9% implied by the heating-value gap is the same size as the 9.1% the model gave.

The same blend rule explains the AFR. Mass-weighting gasoline (about 14.6) and ethanol (9.0) gives a stoichiometric AFR near 13.4 to 13.5 for E20, close to the 13.60 used in the model.

Checked before writing up

  • Emissions are reported as the study report gives them: CO and HC lower, CO2 marginally lower, NOx dependent on engine calibration. No NOx number is quoted.
  • The power loss is quoted only for the corrected-AFR case. Quoting it for the fixed-AFR case would mix a calibration error into a fuel effect.

In progressMSc coursework · ENGR7029 Racing Engine Systems (Thermal) · Sep to Nov 2026

Data-driven modelling of cycle-to-cycle combustion variation in a GDI engine

Measured cylinder pressure from a 1.6 L turbocharged GDI engine, recorded with AVL IndiCom, at nine operating points (2000 to 2800 rpm, 40 to 80 Nm, 100 cycles each) is analysed in MATLAB and used to calibrate a single-cylinder GT-SUITE model. The coursework then tests a published statistical pressure model against this data.

Combustion analysis (MATLAB)

  • Pressure pegging and heat release.
  • Mass fraction burned by Rassweiler-Withrow and Wiebe fits.
  • CA10, CA50 and CA90, and COV of IMEP.

GT-SUITE model

  • Single-cylinder model calibrated to the test-cell data.
  • Cycle-to-cycle variation included.
  • Douaud-Eyzat knock model.

Statistical model

  • Principal component and Gaussian process pressure model (Vlaswinkel and Willems, Energies 2024), implemented and critically evaluated.
  • Tests whether a method developed for RCCI combustion transfers to SI, and whether correlated component weights improve prediction of cyclic spread.
  • PCA weights linked to combustion phasing and burn duration, to give the statistical model a physical meaning.

Coursework in progress: the setup is shown here and results are not reported while marks are pending. Skills used: MATLAB, GT-SUITE, combustion analysis, cylinder pressure analysis, AVL IndiCom data, principal component analysis, Gaussian process regression, engine calibration.

Basis of the analysis: cylinder volume

Every pressure-trace calculation rests on the cylinder volume at each crank angle. This is the full 720° cycle for a 1.6 L four-cylinder direct-injection engine, computed from the slider-crank relation and checked against a direct geometric calculation of piston position, which agrees to floating-point precision.

Geometry used: bore b 77 mm, stroke s 85.8 mm, connecting rod l 138.4 mm, compression ratio r 10.5.

Motoring, combustion phasing and flame speed

Three ideas carry the combustion analysis. The motoring curve is the reference that separates compression from combustion. CA10, CA50 and CA90 describe where the burn sits and how long it takes. Cycle-to-cycle variation then shows up as a shift of that burn curve, and flame speed is what sets its slope. The three plots below are drawn from the equations on this page to show the idea. They are illustrative shapes, not measured data.

n fitted on the compression stroke
xb(θ) = Qnet(θ)Qnet,max   CAk: xb = k/100Mass fraction burned and burn angles
burn duration = CA90 − CA10
xb = 1 − exp(−6.908 θ − θ0Δθm+1)Wiebe function
θ0 start of burn, Δθ duration, m shape
SL = SL0 TuT0α pp0β (1 − 2.1 ydil)Laminar flame speed
Metghalchi and Keck form; unburned gas temperature Tu, residual fraction ydil
ST ≈ SL + u′Turbulent flame speed, simplest form
u′ is the turbulence intensity
  • Why motoring matters. It fixes the pressure reference and shows whether the pegging and the volume are right before any heat release is calculated.
  • Why the shift matters. If the cycles differ mainly by a shift in phasing, a few components can describe the spread. If the burn duration also changes, the slope changes too. The coursework asks whether the principal component weights follow these two effects.
  • Why flame speed matters. Residual gas, mixture quality and turbulence change the flame speed from cycle to cycle. That moves CA50 and the burn duration, and it is the main handle for calibrating the GT-SUITE combustion model to the test-cell data.

Thermal model of an electric traction motor: oil spray cooling of the Prius end windings

Continuous torque from an electric machine is a thermal limit. I modelled the 2004 Toyota Prius traction motor as a 10-node lumped-parameter thermal network (Mellor, Roberts and Turner, 1991) in OpenModelica, validated it against Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) test data, and used it to ask how much direct oil spray on the end windings is worth, the hottest part of the machine.

−0.5 KEnd-winding error against ORNL at 105 °C coolant, after calibrating one frame conductance
−7.2 KEnd-winding hot spot with oil film coefficient raised from 25 to 250 W/m²K
+15%Estimated continuous torque at the same 166 °C, 117.8 to 135.5 N·m. A model estimate, not a test result.
up to 7.6 KDrift at the other ORNL coolant temperatures: calibration at one point is not full validation
Oil spray case study, 105 °C coolant, 900 rpm, half-machine losses 639 W
h₃, W/m²KR₂₅, K/WEnd winding T₆ChangeHeat to oilTorque at 166 °C
25 (as built, rotor splash)0.69166.0 °C–71 W117.8 N·m
500.35163.1 °C−2.8 K95 W124.1 N·m
1000.17160.8 °C−5.2 K114 W129.9 N·m
250 (direct spray)0.07158.8 °C−7.2 K128 W135.5 N·m

What I built

  • Ten nodes (frame, stator yoke and teeth, slot and end winding, end-region oil and air, air gap, rotor, magnets, shaft), 38 thermal resistances and 10 capacitances, following Mellor's cylinder T-network.
  • Half-machine losses from the ORNL 105 °C coolant test (117.8 N·m, 900 rpm): copper 280 W, iron 283.5 W, mechanical 75.5 W. The heat balance closes: 568 W to the water-glycol plus 71 W to the oil.
  • One frame-to-coolant conductance calibrated (12.0 W/K), then frozen and re-run at 35, 50 and 75 °C coolant.
  • Case study: only the end-region film resistances, R = 1/(h₃A), were changed. An independent Python steady-state solver reproduces the OpenModelica temperatures to 0.01 K.

What I learned

  • Gains level off. Spray moves heat into the oil easily, but the oil circuit rejects it through a fixed conductance, so the oil node warms from 139 to 147 °C. Doubling the oil loop gave −11.3 K. Spray only pays with more oil flow or cooler oil.
  • Structure matters as much as tuning. Adding Mellor's slot-liner path that the base network missed changed the calibrated conductance from 12.0 to 16.8 W/K and the spray benefit from 7.2 to 8.5 K.
  • The torque gain is an estimate. It assumes copper loss ∝ I² and torque ∝ I below base speed, with iron loss fixed. Saturation, inverter limits and demagnetisation are not modelled.

T6,0 with copper loss off
ττ0 = √(166 − T6,0) / (T6 − T6,0)Torque at the same hot spot

CompletePython + MATLAB/Simulink · NASA PCoE cell B0005 · 18650 Li-ion · 168 cycles

Equivalent-circuit model of a Li-ion cell, fitted to NASA ageing data

I built a 2-RC equivalent-circuit model (ECM) of a lithium-ion cell in Simulink and identified its parameters from NASA's B0005 ageing test. The test cycles an 18650 cell (2 Ah rating) at 24 °C: 1.5 A CC-CV charge to 4.2 V, then a 2 A discharge to 2.7 V, until the capacity has fallen by about 30%. The questions were how closely a lumped circuit can follow the measured voltage, and what happens to that accuracy as the cell ages.

2.7 mVVoltage RMSE on the fitted discharge above 5% SOC. 10.4 mV including the end-of-discharge knee.
6.0 mVRMSE above 5% SOC on the next cycle, which the fit never saw, with nothing changed in the model
−28.6%Measured capacity over 168 cycles in 55 days: 1.857 to 1.325 Ah
+16%30 s DC resistance at 50% SOC from the re-identified models: 108 to 125 mΩ
Vt = OCV(z) − R0I − v1 − v2Terminal voltage
dzdt = −I3600 QCoulomb counting
dv1dt = R1(z) I − v1τ1Fast branch
dv2dt = R2 I − v2τ2Slow branch

How it was identified

  • Fitted to cycle 1 as one record: the 2 A discharge, the logged rest, and the 1.5 A CC-CV charge that follows. Two current levels in opposite directions separate the OCV from the resistive drop. A discharge alone cannot do that.
  • Fitted values: a 26-point OCV table (monotonic by construction, dense below 10% SOC), R0, R1(SOC), R2, τ1 and τ2. Nonlinear least squares on log-parameters, from four starting points. All four converged to the same minimum.
  • The discretisation is exact for current that varies linearly between samples. That is what the Simulink From Workspace block feeds the model, so the fitted parameters drop straight into Simulink. A continuous-time check agrees within 2.2 mV.
  • For ageing, the full model was re-identified on every cycle, each fit starting from the previous cycle's result.

What the data showed

  • Fitted R0 is 101 mΩ. A short 3.4 A pulse logged at the start of the next charge gives 96 mΩ directly from ΔV/ΔI, an independent check within 5%.
  • R1 rises from about 35 mΩ in mid-range to 235 mΩ at empty. With a constant R1 the fit left about 37 mV RMSE and missed by nearly 0.3 V in the knee. Making R1 depend on SOC brought that down to 10.4 mV.
  • Run unchanged, the cycle-1 model drifts from 18 mV to 228 mV RMSE as the cell ages. Updating only the capacity roughly halves the error late in life. Re-identifying every cycle holds it at 6 to 17 mV for the whole life.
  • Capacity partly recovers after each long rest in the test (cycles 19, 48, 90). The resistance trend shows small steps at the same points.
Identified parameters, cycle 1 (24 °C)
ParameterValue
Capacity Q1.857 Ah
R0101.0 mΩ
R1 at 100 / 50 / 10 / 0% SOC45.5 / 34.6 / 39.9 / 235 mΩ
τ153.7 s
R2, τ210.3 mΩ, 181 s
RMSE, discharge10.4 mV (2.7 mV above 5% SOC)
RMSE, following charge6.9 mV

Limits. The model is isothermal, but the cell warms from 24 °C to 39–41 °C during each discharge, so the fitted resistances average over that rise. With samples 3 to 19 s apart, nothing faster than a few seconds can be identified, so R0 includes the sub-second polarisation. τ2 is capped at 600 s because only a few minutes of rest are logged after each discharge. Hysteresis is not modelled. Next steps are an Arrhenius term on the resistances, and a check against a drive-cycle dataset such as Oxford's.

Analysis completePiara Agro Industries trailer · beam FE model · time and frequency domain · write-up 13 Oct 2026

Trailer axle for a 1.5 tonne single-axle trailer

For the trailer I worked on at Piara Agro Industries, I designed and drew an 80 × 8 mm steel tube axle with welded stub axles, then built a beam-element model of the axle, wheels, tyres and leaf springs and drove it over a bump, a pothole and a rough road at 50, 80 and 100 km/h. The question was whether it survives single impacts, and where its fatigue life is set.

66 MPaStatic stress at the spring-seat weld. Hand calculation gives 66.4 MPa.
199 MPaAt the 3 g design load, safety factor 1.79 on 355 MPa yield
112 MPaPeak over a 50 mm bump at 40 km/h, 1.7 times static
51,000 kmFatigue life at the seat weld on a class C road. About 636,000 km on class B.

Design

  • Beam: CHS 80 × 8 mm, 1450 mm long, S355J2H, yield 355 MPa.
  • Stub axles: 42CrMo4 quenched and tempered, bearings on d45 and d32.
  • Spring seats: plates 70 × 120 × 12 mm, 6 mm fillet weld, leaf springs clamped with U-bolts.
  • Brake flange d180 × 16 with 4 × d11 on PCD 140.

Result in short

The axle is strong enough for single hits and for the 3 g design case. Its natural bending frequencies, 65 Hz and above, sit well over road input below 20 Hz, so the axle does not resonate by itself. The stress comes from the body bouncing at 1.7 Hz and the wheels hopping at 13.5 Hz. The weakest point is the weld where the spring seat joins the tube, and that weld sets the fatigue life.

Rough road, ISO 8608 class C
SpeedRMS stress at weldBody vibrationTyre force variation
50 km/h11.3 MPa0.16 g±19%
80 km/h14.3 MPa0.20 g±25%
100 km/h16.0 MPa0.22 g±28%

Checks on the model

  • Static stress at the weld: 66.2 MPa in the model against 66.4 MPa by hand, 0.3% apart.
  • First free-free bending mode: 139.9 Hz against 137.8 Hz from beam theory, 1.5% apart.
  • Four mesh sizes gave the same 114.2 Hz clamped-seat mode.
  • Random-road RMS stress: 14.4 MPa from the time run and 14.3 MPa from the frequency method.
  • Fatigue: 51,000 km by rainflow counting and 65,000 km by the Dirlik method, the same order.

What would improve it

  • CHS 90 × 8 tube: about 24% less stress and roughly double the fatigue life.
  • Move the spring seats outward to shorten the 300 mm lever arm.
  • Grind the weld toes.
Limits. Spring rate, tyre stiffness and masses are assumed values, not measurements. The model is a planar beam model, so fore-aft braking bending is a hand calculation. Interleaf friction is treated as viscous damping, and bump stops are not modelled. Fatigue uses the IIW FAT 71 curve for an as-welded attachment with no extra safety factor. A SolidWorks 2024 frequency study is set up to confirm the 114 Hz mode, and its result is not shown here.

Design and first-pass analysisBusiness idea · parametric CAD · hand calculation and simplified models

Soapbox racing series: a build-and-race kit for families

The idea is a UK soapbox racing series where families buy a durable, ready-to-assemble kit, build the cart together in a day, personalise it and race it in regional heats. I modelled a Stock class cart for ages 8 to 12 in CAD and ran a first engineering pass on its aerodynamics, crash behaviour and frame strength, to steer the design before any physical test.

100.4 kgCart 55.4 kg from CAD volumes, plus a 45 kg driver
2.7%Gradient at which the cart reaches a 30 km/h terminal speed
298 to 476 gDeceleration with the carbon crash nose as first drawn. Rejected.
FoS 0.88Ash frame, 20 g hit on one rail. Drives the front-bay stiffening.

The business idea

Target market

UK families with middle-to-upper-middle incomes. Parents are the paying customers who want quality family time and hands-on STEM learning. Their children and teenagers, 4 to 16 and over, build, race and drive.

What makes it different

The only UK soapbox experience that takes families from build to race: a kit built together in a day, personalised, and raced in a regional series and a national final. Working slogan: Build it together. Make it yours. Race it for real.

Promotion

  • Own-brand casual clothing (hoodies, T-shirts, caps) and stickers.
  • A website for orders and event information.
  • TikTok, Instagram and Facebook.
  • Retail channels, such as Amazon, still to be decided.

Pricing and the sales plan are still being worked out. Kit contents, safety and the competitions will set the price.

The cart

Ash timber ladder frame (two 45 × 70 mm rails, five cross-members and a 40 mm diagonal brace), 2.5 mm CFRP body shell, bolt-on CFRP crash nose, roll hoop, 250 mm pneumatic tyres. The model is parametric (CadQuery) with a STEP file for each part, so rail sizes and wheelbase can be changed and re-run.

First-pass analysis

  • The carbon nose as drawn is far too stiff. A 3 mm CFRP cone crushes at a mean 293 to 469 kN, which is 298 to 476 g on a 100 kg cart and child. The energy it can absorb is fine; the force is the problem. Use the carbon as a thin fairing over an EPP foam absorber.
  • The course, not the cart, must limit speed. A 30 km/h stop at a mean 20 g needs 177 mm of crush, and at 10 g it needs 354 mm. The cart reaches 30 km/h on a 2.7% gradient, so series courses should be gentle, about 3 to 4%, with straw-bale or tyre run-off.
  • The ash frame is fine for normal running and needs care in a crash. A 3 g bump gives 5.31 MPa (factor of safety 18.8). A 20 g frontal stop gives 1.31 for a square hit but 0.88 when one rail takes it, so stiffen the front bay with gussets or deeper rails.
  • The driver dominates drag. Drag only overtakes rolling resistance (14.8 N) above about 30 km/h. A streamlined body and a flat-fronted box differ by about 7% in the 2D flow check, because the wake behind the helmet and roll hoop sets most of the drag. A head fairing and closed tail are the next gains.
  • A single-skin 2.5 mm side wall is too flexible. An adult leaning 700 N on it gives about 739 MPa against a 500 MPa strength. Use a foam-cored sandwich or a bonded sill flange.

Design changes this led to

  • EPP foam absorber sized for 10 to 15 g behind a thin 0.8 to 1 mm fairing.
  • Course speed cap of about 30 km/h through gradient and run-off.
  • Foam-cored sandwich body, at least at the cockpit sill and sides.
  • Steel gussets or 45 × 90 mm rails in the front bay, with glued halving joints plus through-bolts.
  • Helmet fairing behind the roll hoop and a closed tail, checked in 3D.

Next checks

  • SolidWorks Simulation: frame and roll-hoop static checks, drop test.
  • SolidWorks Flow Simulation: 3D external aero with a modelled driver.
  • Physical crush test of the foam nose and a weighed prototype.
Limits. These are hand calculations and simplified models: timber treated as isotropic along the grain, crush as an ideal square pulse, 2D flow at a much lower Reynolds number than reality, and the driver as simple shapes. The drag coefficients are assumptions. No physical testing has been done, and no child should drive the cart before it has been tested.

CompleteGT-SUITE · turbocharged 1.6 L V6 · Monza drive cycle

Turbocharged 1.6 L V6 against the 2026 power unit rules

I modelled a turbocharged 1.6 L V6 over the Monza circuit to look at compressor map operation and boost response under racing loads, and evaluated the engine's power against the MGU-K torque and battery constraints set by the 2026 FIA power unit rules.

The 2026 power unit, in brief

  • Engine stays a 1.6 L turbocharged V6.
  • MGU-H removed.
  • MGU-K output rises from 120 kW to up to 350 kW, so electrical power is close to half of peak.
  • Braking energy recovery rises to roughly 8.5 MJ per lap.

Sources: Honda F1 regulation commentary, The Race, Formula1.com.

Why it changes the engine job

With the MGU-H gone, the turbo can no longer be driven or braked electrically, so boost response comes back to the compressor map and the exhaust energy alone. A larger MGU-K shifts peak demand to the battery and e-machine limits, which is the constraint set the engine has to be sized against.

PR = p02p01Compressor pressure ratio
ηc = T01(PR(γ−1)/γ − 1)T02 − T01Isentropic efficiency
ṁcorr = ṁ√(T01/Tref)p01/prefCorrected mass flow
02 - Test cell

Engine R&D at Eicher Engines

TMTL Eicher Engines Centre of Excellence, Alwar. January to June 2025. Three workstreams.

Durability testing in the test cell

500-hour RPT durability cycle on a three-cylinder engine, run on the dynamometer. I worked on it from the test run through to the post-test teardown, and evaluated the results against the compliance requirements.

During the test

  • Ran the engine on the dynamometer through the 500 h RPT cycle.
  • Logged engine data through the test-cell data acquisition (National Instruments).
  • Compared the results with the compliance requirements.

After the test

  • Took engine oil samples and sent them to the company for analysis.
  • Weighed the engine parts and compared with their weight before the test.
  • Inspected the bearings and the crankshaft.

What it tells you

  • Mass lost per part over 500 h gives its wear rate.
  • Oil analysis results come from the company lab, not from me.
  • Bearing and crankshaft condition shows whether the engine finished the cycle in an acceptable state.

Other workstreams

Valvetrain dynamics

Built Ricardo VALDYN valvetrain models for a three-cylinder engine and compared rocker-pushrod configurations through dynamic behaviour analysis. Generated cam profiles and evaluated valve lift, acceleration and contact dynamics to improve valvetrain performance.

Emissions and aftertreatment to CPCB IV+

Ran durability and emissions testing on diesel genset engines against CPCB IV+ norms and checked performance against the compliance requirements. Analysed test results from genset and tractor engines.

Worked on the exhaust aftertreatment system (ATS): checked for excess urea (DEF) dosing, and used a borescope to inspect the white urea deposits that build up inside the ATS.

Builds

Oxford Brookes Racing

Formula Student · Feb 2026 to present

Powertrain and composites team member. On powertrain I work on traction control development and testing, and assemble powertrain and chassis parts with the other sub-system teams to fixed competition deadlines.

On composites I work on the test rig used to prove the structural equivalency of the car's composite structures for the Formula Student Structural Equivalency Spreadsheet (SES).

Baja SAE powertrain

Team Ultron Motorsports · Dec 2022 to Nov 2024

Designed the rear-wheel-drive powertrain for an ATV built around a Briggs and Stratton 305 cc, 10 HP engine: drivetrain calculations, component selection, CVT tuning and casing fabrication.

Worked out gradability, approach and ramp-over angles, improved braking response by bleeding the brakes for consistent pressure, and supported the team at ATVC 2024.

Trailer chassis, drone transport

Piara Agro Industries · Feb to Mar 2025

Modelled the trailer and chassis in PTC Creo from physical measurements with DFM and DOE, and ran modal and time-domain FEA.

Took it from drawing approval through a full pass of trailer and axle structural testing to a production-ready chassis for utility and drone-transport use.

EV roller test rig

Final year project · Thapar Institute

Designed and built an EV chassis roller test rig and logged battery voltage, current and temperature under variable load to study battery behaviour.

BMW M52 intake manifold

GT-SUITE · CAD

Reverse-engineered the intake manifold and simulated airflow, pressure behaviour and engine breathing.

Conventional and hybrid drive-cycle models

ENGR7005 coursework · GT-SUITE · Python

Built a custom drive cycle from GPS data on an Oxford route (city, Headington, Wheatley, Cowley), then ran GT-SUITE models of a VW Lupo and a 2004 Toyota Prius power-split hybrid over eight drive cycles.

The hybrid used 4.76 to 6.94 L/100 km, with its engine operating points held near the minimum BSFC line. A DOE gear-shift optimisation cut the conventional car's fuel use on the custom cycle from 7.7 to 6.47 L/100 km.
